phase1.explanation:
The storage room is organized. Every program up to this point, though, has still been one worker in that workshop, doing one thing at a time, start to finish. [[key:multithreading is what happens when you put more than one worker in the workshop at once, all reaching for the same shelves]] — and that's a genuinely different kind of programming, not just "the same code, faster."

A running Java program is a [[term:process]] — its own chunk of memory, isolated from every other program on the machine. A [[term:thread]] is a worker inside that process. [[fun:every program you've written so far has had exactly one thread — the main thread]] — main() runs top to bottom on it, one instruction after another, and that's been the entire mental model since Unit 1.

Multithreading means multiple threads running inside the same process, and [[warn:the part that makes this genuinely new is what they share]]: every thread gets its own stack (its own local variables, its own call history), but they all share the same heap — the same objects, the same instance fields, the same collections you spent this whole unit organizing. Two workers reaching into the same storage bin at the same instant is exactly the kind of situation ordinary single-threaded code was never written to survive.

[[key:why bother, then?]] Two real reasons: parallelism — genuinely doing independent work at the same time on a multi-core CPU, like processing four image files simultaneously instead of one after another — and responsiveness — keeping an app's main thread free to react to input while a slow task (a big file download, a database query) runs somewhere else instead of freezing everything. [[warn:more threads is not automatically faster]] — on a single core, threads don't run truly simultaneously at all, they take turns so quickly it looks simultaneous, and coordinating between them (which the rest of this unit covers) has a real cost of its own.

phase2.explanation:
Conceptual lesson — no broken code!

Common misconception: "More threads always means better performance."

Actually: More threads can reduce performance due to:
• Context switching overhead
• Memory consumption
• Increased complexity
• Limited CPU cores

Recommendation: Number of threads ≈ Number of CPU cores (for CPU-bound tasks)

Another misconception: "Threads are completely independent and don't interact."

Actually: Threads share memory and resources. This is what causes race conditions and deadlocks!

Example of a race condition:
Two threads both increment a shared counter: counter++
Thread A reads counter (5), Thread B reads counter (5)
Both increment (6), both write (6) — Should be 7!

Always use synchronization when sharing data between threads!

phase3.openingDialogue: Multithreading — doing multiple things at once! 🧵

mcq.question:
Which statement about multithreading is TRUE?

A) Adding more threads always makes a program faster
B) Threads share memory and can access the same data
C) A process cannot have multiple threads
D) All threads run in parallel on all CPUs
E) Threads never interact with each other

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: The number of hardware threads actually available on a machine is Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() — but that number is a hint, not a hard cap. Java happily lets you create thousands of Thread objects on a 4-core machine; the OS scheduler just switches between them faster than any human could notice, which is exactly the illusion of "simultaneous" this lesson is getting at.
